extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level exposition of the principles and distinctions governing induction (perfect vs imperfect) and the logical foundations of number, aimed at explaining when inductive inferences are warranted and how numerical reasoning relates to logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect Induction (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Induction is called perfect when all the objects or events which can possibly come under the class treated have been examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect Induction is 'absolutely requisite' both for performing imperfect induction and for treating large bodies of facts whose knowledge is complete. Even when it gives no new information, its condensation and abbreviation of particulars is essential for mental economy and for making general statements about fully examined domains (examples: all teeth of an animal, all strata in a geological section, all coins in a hoard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Induction (definition and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect Induction is used when it is impossible to examine all instances; it involves uncertainty and proceeds from observed instances to unexamined ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperfect Induction is founded on Perfect Induction but 'involves another process of inference of a widely different character.' Its conclusions are hypothetical and never more than probable; it 'never makes any real addition to our knowledge' but unfolds what was implicit in prior observations. Examples show where it is unsafe (e.g., cryptogamous plants with mixed structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from Perfect to Imperfect Induction (warrant for generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage from conclusions limited to observed data to conclusions that apply beyond those data is a profound question requiring grounds for warranting inference from known to unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a step appears to 'gain a net addition to our knowledge' but is actually hypothetical and depends on assumptions that past observations are representative and that conditions remain unchanged; the author promises detailed discussion of the principles justifying this passage in later sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental assumptions underlying inductive inference
rubrics_metrics.description: All inferences to unexamined objects and times proceed on two assumptions: (1) that our past observation gives us a complete knowledge of what exists; (2) that the conditions of things which did exist will continue to be the conditions which will exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions are essential to imperfect induction but are philosophically problematic because we know only a point of the Universe in space and time and cannot estimate the probability of arbitrary changes in the world's constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for certainty of prediction (ballot-box analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty of prediction depends on (1) acquiring perfect knowledge of the comparative numbers of 'kinds' within the system and (2) the contents/constitution remaining unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the infinite ballot-box simile, science registers frequencies to infer future drawings; but certainty requires both perfect knowledge of proportions and stability of the box's contents. The latter is a metaphysical assumption about no arbitrary change in the Universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of number and probability in imperfect induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When passing beyond certainty, number and quantity enter inference: probability (based on counts/frequencies) becomes the measure grounding inductive claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift from logical certainty to probabilistic reasoning is not a departure from logic; number and quantity are treated as parts of the logical domain and used to estimate probabilities of future occurrences given observed frequencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary principles about imperfect induction (four-point summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly stated conclusions regarding imperfect induction: (1) it rests upon perfect induction for materials; (2) the apparent passage from examined to unexamined is an inverse application of deductive inference; (3) the result is always hypothetical and never more than probable; (4) reasoning never makes a net addition to knowledge—the future is only the unfolded contents of previous knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These points are presented as guiding doctrines to keep in mind throughout subsequent treatment of imperfect induction and its application to investigations of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number as logical discrimination (nature of number)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number is 'but another name for diversity': plurality arises only when difference is detected; a unit is any object of thought which can be discriminated from every other object treated as a unit in the same problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units must be discriminable; repetition of the same name has no effect in logic (Law of Unity). Examples: counting coins requires counting each coin once; counting in time (beats of a pendulum) uses temporal discrimination. The logical definition of unit grounds numerical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Unity and logical conditions for counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical Law of Unity: repeated identical names in logical symbols have no effect (A + A = A); in counting, identical alternatives must be reduced before counting to avoid false plurality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to apply this leads to counting errors (counting the same coin twice) and misapplication of numerical operations; logical attention to identity/difference is prerequisite to valid numerical calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical abstraction vs logical abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical abstraction consists in abstracting the fact of difference that gives rise to plurality while ignoring the character of those differences; logical abstraction drops the existence of difference (unity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract number asserts existence of discriminations without specifying them (e.g., 'three' in general), enabling broad generalizations and the foundation of mathematical reasoning. Concrete number specifies the logical characters (e.g., three coins, three men).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete and abstract number (homogeneity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete number specifies the logical characters of items counted, while abstract number does not; numerical calculations require homogeneity of the logical nature of items (Law of Homogeneity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot properly add heterogeneous units (yards and pounds) in the same sum unless they are reduced to a common denominator or kept distinct in a compound calculation. Examples: chemistry equations treat atoms of different kinds as separate but parallel equations; compound mathematical equations are equivalent to several separate equations for each unit-kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Homogeneity (units' logical nature must remain unaltered)
rubrics_metrics.description: In every arithmetical calculation the logical nature of the things numbered must remain unaltered; specified logical agreement must not be affected by unspecified numerical differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arithmetic that mixes units of different kinds without reduction is absurd (e.g., adding length to time). In complex calculations, different units are kept distinct and treated numerically only in conjunction with their own kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy and limits between logical and numerical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical symbols and operations obey many laws analogous to logical laws (commutativity, etc.), but there are important distinctions (e.g., simplicity law AA = A has different implications in number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy supports that number arises from logical conditions, but cautions are given where direct analogy fails (examples with multiplication and units discriminations). The mathematician must remain within prior conditions of logical correctness for validity.
